name: Tesler's Law
description: For any system, there is a certain amount of complexity that cannot be reduced — it can only be moved between the user and the system/developer.
design_relevance_note: Commonly invoked to justify design trade-offs between simplicity and hidden complexity.
myth_risk_note: Tesler's Law of Conservation of Complexity is a recognized principle attributed to Xerox designer Larry Tesler and widely cited in UX education and practice, but no peer-reviewed empirical validation or direct testing of this principle was found in the discovery data.
prevalence_note: Known among more experienced practitioners as the 'law of conservation of complexity,' less universally cited than Jakob's or Fitts's Law.

applications.title: Larry Tesler's Xerox PARC realization behind the Law of Conservation of Complexity
applications.description: While working at Xerox PARC in the mid-1980s, Larry Tesler (later at Apple, credited with popularizing cut/copy/paste and modeless interface design) argued that an engineer should spend an extra week reducing an application's inherent complexity rather than force millions of users to each spend an extra minute dealing with that same complexity -- the origin of the principle that a system's total complexity is conserved and must be absorbed by either the system's designers or its users, never eliminated.
applications.industry_context: enterprise software / early GUI design (Xerox PARC)
applications.ethical_note: A pure engineering-tradeoff principle -- who absorbs unavoidable complexity, the system's builders or its users -- with no persuasion or manipulation dimension. Straightforwardly user-beneficial in its stated intent (push complexity away from the user, toward the engineering effort), included as the corpus's first real-world grounding for this heuristic's origin rather than leaving it with zero practical illustration.
